planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring beneath conifers or oaks in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; established colonies tolerate the dry summer shade typical of West Coast forest floors better than most eastern wild gingers.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil beneath conifers or oaks in partial to full shade. Hartweg's wild ginger is a California and southern Oregon native prized for its handsome, silver-marbled, heart-shaped evergreen leaves, which form a low, slow-creeping mat rarely more than a few inches tall. The dark maroon, cup-shaped flowers open at ground level in early spring, tucked beneath the foliage where they attract small pollinating flies and beetles. It tolerates dry summer shade better than many eastern wild gingers once established, making it a natural underplanting for redwoods, Douglas fir, and native oaks.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or fall in rich, evenly moist, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; space 10-15 inches apart and mulch with leaf litter to conserve moisture through the growing season.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or fall in rich, evenly moist, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade. Siebold's wild ginger is a deciduous East Asian species native to Korea, Japan, and northeastern China, forming clumps of soft, arrow-shaped, deep green leaves that are sometimes marbled with silver depending on provenance. The small, three-lobed, purplish-brown flowers open at soil level in early spring before the new leaves fully expand. Long grown in Korea and China for its pungent, aromatic root, it is equally valuable in North American gardens simply as a refined, cold-hardy groundcover for shaded borders.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full to partial shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind; part the foliage occasionally to check for the distinctive flowers hidden at soil level.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full to partial shade, sheltered from winter wind. 'Ling Ling' is a selection of the Chinese species Asarum maximum grown chiefly for its extraordinary flowers — large, glossy, deep purple-black cups with a wide white-edged throat that resemble a small panda's face when viewed from above, produced at ground level beneath the broad, glossy evergreen leaves in early spring. Gently part the foliage in spring to view the blooms, since like other Asarum species they are borne low to the soil and easily overlooked. Less cold-hardy than American or European wild gingers, it performs best in warm-temperate gardens with reliably moist, humus-rich soil and protection from harsh winter exposure.
